name: shtools
why: Spherical harmonic tools for geophysics and planetary maps lets you run real science on a globe at home.

brief.what_it_is: SHTOOLS (the Python package is called pyshtools, docs show version 4.14) is a library for working with spherical harmonics on a sphere. It takes gridded data or spherical harmonic coefficients as input and returns transforms between them, spectra, and derived fields. Its stated uses are spherical harmonic transforms, multitaper spectral analyses, expansion of gridded data into Slepian basis functions, and standard operations on global gravity and magnetic field data. The core is Fortran 95, wrapped by a Python interface, and it also imports gravity, topography and magnetic datasets and makes maps via Cartopy and PyGMT. It is a code library, not a command-line tool, so it has no executables.
brief.why_it_exists: The README describes it as an archive of software for spherical harmonic transforms, multitaper spectral analysis and Slepian expansions of global gravitational and magnetic field data. The reference paper is Wieczorek and Meschede (2018), SHTools: Tools for working with spherical harmonics, in Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems.
brief.how_it_works: The Fortran 95 core runs the transforms and is exposed to Python through wrappers and dedicated classes. Users can pick among normalization and phase conventions and convert between real and complex harmonics, and the README mentions a choice of backends (the native Fortran one, or DUCC0) for the heavy math. The docs also describe regularly sampled geographic grids and Gauss-Legendre quadrature grids.

brief.install_notes: For Python, pip or conda is the normal route, and pre-built binaries are said to exist for Linux, macOS and Windows. The conda route is listed as Linux and macOS only. Building from source needs a Fortran compiler and build tools: gfortran, cmake and build-essential on Debian/Ubuntu, the C development tools on Fedora/RHEL, and xcode-select --install on macOS. The developer path also uses a conda environment.yml. The brew and macports packages install the Fortran library, not the Python package. The docs have an Installing page for further options, which I did not open.
brief.standout: Fortran 95 core with a Python API, plus Slepian and multitaper tools, which are uncommon in general-purpose Python science packages. It also builds on well-known tools such as xarray, netCDF, Cartopy and PyGMT for making maps.
brief.status: Unknown on dates: I saw no last-release or last-commit date. The docs are at pyshtools 4.14, the README points to a develop/master release workflow, and it links a Zenodo DOI and a Binder/Matrix chat, so it looks actively maintained, but this is not confirmed.
brief.caveats: The Fortran brew/macports packages are a different thing from the Python pyshtools package, so the brew line in the README can confuse people who want Python. Conda is listed for Linux and macOS only. Building from source needs a compiler toolchain. The README says the native Fortran backend is accurate up to about degree 2800, and beyond that you need the DUCC0 backend. The README calls the Fortran build paths for Windows through brew, which I did not verify. The Fortran reference documentation is a separate site linked from the homepage.

entry.title: SHTOOLS
entry.tldr: A Fortran 95 library, with a Python interface, for spherical harmonics: transform gravity, magnetic and topography maps of whole planets into frequencies and back.
entry.deeper_look:
SHTOOLS works with data on a sphere. Give it a global grid or a set of spherical harmonic coefficients and it transforms between the two, computes power spectra, and produces derived fields. Spherical harmonics are to a globe what Fourier series are to a time signal: they split a map into patterns of increasing spatial detail.

It was built for geophysics and planetary science. The README describes an archive of software for spherical harmonic transforms, multitaper spectral analysis, Slepian expansions, and standard operations on global gravity and magnetic field data. The reference paper is Wieczorek and Meschede (2018) in Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems. The numerical core is Fortran 95, wrapped for Python as pyshtools. It can import gravity, topography and magnetic datasets and draw maps through Cartopy and PyGMT.

The idea underneath is that a field on a sphere can be analysed like a signal. Slepian functions, for example, concentrate that analysis on one region, such as a continent, when you do not have data for the whole globe. You can choose among normalization and phase conventions, convert between real and complex harmonics, and pick a native Fortran or DUCC0 backend for the heavy math.

This is a library, not a command-line tool. The brew formula installs the Fortran library only, and it has no executables. To play with it you almost certainly want the Python package.
entry.install:
pip install pyshtools
# the brew formula installs only the Fortran library, not the Python package:
brew install shtools
# alternative: conda install -c conda-forge pyshtools (Linux and macOS only)
# Building from source needs a Fortran compiler and build tools.

entry.whats_unique: It pairs a Fortran 95 core with a Python API and includes multitaper and Slepian tools, which are uncommon in general-purpose Python science packages.
entry.caveats: The brew and MacPorts packages are the Fortran library, not the Python package, which is easy to mix up; the native backend is accurate to about degree 2800, and beyond that DUCC0 is needed.
